finding: The RISE FOR HEALTH treatment figure is a percentage of all 3,000 analyzed participants, not the subset with symptoms; the current wording changes its denominator.
evidence: Original study abstract reproduced by Washington University: https://profiles.wustl.edu/en/publications/lower-urinary-tract-symptoms-in-us-women-contemporary-prevalence-/ (DOI 10.1097/JU.0000000000004009): of 3,000 eligible participants, 79% had LUTS and 7.1% of participants reported treatment. A later PLUS Consortium report confirms the participant denominator: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/nau.70230.

edit.old: only 7.1% of women with symptoms had received treatment
edit.new: only 7.1% of all 3,000 participants reported treatment for LUTS

finding: The levator-avulsion meta-analysis gives the unadjusted pooled SUI odds-ratio upper confidence limit as 1.34, not 1.30.
evidence: Opened full text, Smeets et al., DOI 10.1002/ijgo.13496: https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ijgo.13496. Seven studies, 2,388 women; pooled OR 0.87 (95% CI 0.56–1.34), adjusted OR 0.72 (0.40–1.30).

finding: The cited joint-hypermobility review supports the stated prolapse, incontinence and perioperative observations for JHS/hEDS, but the row extends those findings to Marfan syndrome without support from that source.
evidence: Opened PubMed abstract PMID 41512700, DOI 10.1016/j.ejogrb.2026.114943: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41512700/. Its population is joint hypermobility syndrome, also called hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome; it does not address Marfan syndrome.

edit.old: | **Connective tissue disorders** | Joint hypermobility syndrome / hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and Marfan syndrome are associated with more than twice the risk of pelvic organ prolapse and high rates of stress and urgency incontinence; affected women often present younger and carry added perioperative considerations (tissue fragility, impaired wound healing)<sup>[[21]](#ref21)</sup> |
edit.new: | **Joint hypermobility syndrome / hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome** | A narrative review reports an association with more than twice the risk of pelvic organ prolapse and high rates of stress and urgency incontinence; some series describe tissue fragility and impaired wound healing relevant to operative planning.<sup>[[21]](#ref21)</sup> |

finding: The 597-woman urodynamic cohort did not provide 597 valid VLPP and MUCP values; naming the measurement denominators keeps the correlation finding in its actual analyzed population.
evidence: Opened publisher abstract, Nager et al., DOI 10.1002/nau.20836: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/nau.20836. Among 597 enrolled women, 372 had valid VLPP and 539 had valid MUCP/FUL values.

edit.old: A secondary analysis of a 597-woman midurethral-sling trial population found that urethral-function urodynamic measures (VLPP, MUCP)
edit.new: A secondary analysis of a 597-woman midurethral-sling trial population (valid VLPP n = 372; MUCP n = 539) found that urethral-function urodynamic measures (VLPP, MUCP)

finding: The caffeine row turns an observational association with detrusor instability at more than 400 mg/day into a one-cup threshold and an elimination recommendation on an SUI page. The cited study did not establish causality or benefit from caffeine reduction for stress leakage.
evidence: Opened PubMed abstract PMID 10862848, DOI 10.1016/s0029-7844(00)00808-5: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10862848/. High intake >400 mg/day was associated with detrusor instability (OR 2.4, 95% CI 1.1–6.5); 100–400 mg/day was nonsignificant. EAU female LUTS 2026 says caffeine reduction may improve urgency/frequency but not incontinence: https://uroweb.org/guidelines/non-neurogenic-female-luts/chapter/disease-management.

edit.old: | **Caffeine reduction** | Even 1 cup/day associated with incontinence; trial of elimination warranted. A case-control study found high intake (>400 mg/day) an independent risk factor for detrusor instability (OR 2.4, 95% CI 1.1–6.5) after controlling for age and smoking, which is the mechanistic rationale when urgency coexists with SUI<sup>[[20]](#ref20)</sup> |
edit.new: | **Caffeine reduction** | When urgency or frequency coexists with SUI, a reduction trial may help those symptoms; benefit for stress leakage is unproven. A case-control study associated >400 mg/day with detrusor instability (OR 2.4, 95% CI 1.1–6.5), an urgency-related endpoint, without establishing causality.<sup>[[20]](#ref20)[[15]](#ref15)</sup> |

finding: The prolapse examination row misses the operative decision it creates: reduction testing for occult SUI in a continent woman before prolapse surgery, followed by counseling about concomitant versus staged continence treatment.
evidence: Opened EAU female LUTS 2026 disease-management guideline, section 4.7.3: https://uroweb.org/guidelines/non-neurogenic-female-luts/chapter/disease-management. It gives a Strong recommendation to perform a POP-reduction test in continent women to identify occult SUI and counsel about adding anti-incontinence surgery; SUI after reduction occurred in up to about 30% in cited series.

edit.old: | Pelvic organ prolapse | May mask or worsen SUI; assess all three compartments |
edit.new: | Pelvic organ prolapse | Assess all compartments. Before planned prolapse surgery in a continent woman, perform a reduction cough stress test for occult SUI and counsel about concomitant versus staged continence treatment.<sup>[[15]](#ref15)</sup> |

finding: A one-day voiding diary is shorter than the current EAU minimum for standardized female LUTS assessment; the page should retain the diary's diagnostic role while specifying at least three days.
evidence: Opened EAU female LUTS 2026 diagnosis guideline, section 3.3: https://uroweb.org/guidelines/non-neurogenic-female-luts/chapter/diagnosis. Bladder diaries of 3–7 days are reliable; 'Use a bladder diary with a duration of ≥3 days' is Strong.

edit.old: A 1–3 day fluid intake and voiding diary identifies modifiable factors (total intake, caffeine, nocturnal patterns) and quantifies leakage frequency when history is insufficient.<sup>[[3]](#ref3)</sup>
edit.new: A bladder diary of at least three days records fluid intake, voiding, urgency, leakage and pad use during assessment and follow-up.<sup>[[15]](#ref15)</sup>

finding: Calling pregnancy SUI usually self-limited can understate persistent postpartum risk; the cited review specifically reports greater postpartum UI risk among women who leaked during pregnancy.
evidence: Opened full review, Sangsawang and Sangsawang, DOI 10.1007/s00192-013-2061-7: https://rcastoragev2.blob.core.windows.net/c53ea79a5bd8ebb176077ffaace5502c/PMC3671107.pdf. The introduction states that UI during pregnancy increases risk of permanent postpartum or later-life incontinence, and women with pregnancy UI have higher postpartum UI risk than women without it.

edit.old: SUI is the most common type of urinary incontinence during pregnancy itself, usually a distinct, self-limited presentation rather than the adult-onset or postsurgical SUI discussed above.
edit.new: SUI is the most common type of urinary incontinence during pregnancy. Symptoms may improve after delivery, but pregnancy-associated leakage is linked to a higher risk of postpartum incontinence.

finding: A nonsignificant between-procedure comparison in a secondary analysis does not establish that operation choice cannot influence sexual outcome.
evidence: Opened PubMed abstract PMID 31923066, DOI 10.1097/AOG.0000000000003648: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31923066/. The secondary analysis of 924 SISTEr/TOMUS participants found mean PISQ-12 improvement through 24 months and no statistically significant between-procedure difference after adjustment.

edit.old: Counsel that sexual function commonly improves after SUI surgery but is not guaranteed to, and that procedure choice among these four options is not a determinant of sexual outcome.
edit.new: Counsel that sexual function improved on average in these trial cohorts, while individual outcomes vary; this secondary analysis detected no statistically significant difference in 24-month PISQ-12 scores among the four operations.

finding: The mesh note uses 'regulatory approval' for SUI slings and treats the FDA's 2011 safety communication as a restriction. These devices use FDA clearance, while the 2019 stop-selling order concerned transvaginal mesh for prolapse.
evidence: Opened FDA history: https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/urogynecologic-surgical-mesh-implants/fdas-activities-urogynecologic-surgical-mesh. It calls July 2011 a POP-mesh safety communication, April 2019 a stop-selling order for transvaginal POP mesh, and says SUI mesh remained class II. An FDA 510(k) record documents clearance for an SUI midurethral sling: https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfpmn/pmn.cfm?ID=K052175.

edit.old: FDA actions (2011, 2019) restricted transvaginal mesh for prolapse but midurethral slings for SUI retain regulatory approval given favorable risk-benefit data.
edit.new: The FDA's 2011 safety communication and 2019 stop-selling order concerned transvaginal mesh for prolapse; they did not prohibit midurethral slings for SUI, which remain FDA-cleared devices.

finding: The ISD paragraph presents a 20–60 cmH₂O MUCP range as if pressure thresholds define the mechanism. EAU describes poor diagnostic accuracy and advises against using urethral pressure testing to grade SUI severity.
evidence: Opened EAU female LUTS 2026 disease-management guideline, section 4.2.3: https://uroweb.org/guidelines/non-neurogenic-female-luts/chapter/disease-management. MUCP reproducibility is conflicting, recording methods are not meaningfully comparable, and 'Do not use urethral pressure profilometry or leak point pressure to grade severity of incontinence' is Strong.

edit.old: Loss of intrinsic urethral mucosal and muscular tone results in poor urethral coaptation and a reduced resting urethral closure pressure (<20–60 cmH₂O depending on criteria).
edit.new: Intrinsic sphincter deficiency involves poor urethral coaptation; MUCP may be low, but a single pressure cutoff does not reliably define the phenotype or grade SUI severity.<sup>[[15]](#ref15)</sup>

finding: The numbered checklist makes supervised PFMT appear to be a required step before surgery, contrary to this page's earlier statement and the AUA/SUFU list of treatment choices.
evidence: Opened local AUA/SUFU 2023 unabridged female SUI guideline (the page's ref 10), Patient Counseling Statement 8, Clinical Principle: counsel about observation, PFMT, other nonsurgical options and surgery. The page itself says conservative-treatment failure is not a universal surgical prerequisite: line 160; the linked treatment database says patients need not progress through every option.

edit.old: 5. **First-line:** Prescribe supervised PFMT ± lifestyle modifications (weight loss, caffeine reduction)
edit.new: 5. **Conservative option:** Offer supervised PFMT and appropriate lifestyle measures according to patient goals; surgery need not await PFMT failure.

evidence: Opened repository STYLE.md section 3: the lead should define the subject and should not say 'This page covers'. The adjacent treatment-database link remains available.
